strengths: Explores a genuinely interesting direction: extending mask-based discrete diffusion (Dream-7B) to a unified any-to-any multimodal model spanning text, speech, and images, with a single joint distribution over multimodal discrete tokens rather than an LLM plus external output heads.

The system is non-trivial and largely well-engineered: a three-stage progressive training pipeline, attenuated tail-pad masking for variable-length generation, position penalty for image decoding order, special token pre-infilling, and adaptive token-length assignment for ASR/TTS.

Reports a constructed SDVI dataset (30K spoken-VQA + 30K speech-to-image) with a reasonable data-quality pipeline (filtering math/code, rewriting MCQs, voice cloning with varied speakers), which is a useful artifact for the community.
Visual understanding results are reasonably strong for a 7B model (POPE 76.6, MME-P 1216.7, Seed-2-Plus 34.5), competitive with specialized visual LLMs and above prior any-to-any models.

Demonstrates two intrinsic advantages of diffusion over AR: free inpainting without fine-tuning and graceful degradation with few sampling steps (Tab. 3, Figs. 6-7), which is a meaningful qualitative point.
The probabilistic formulation (Eq. 1) and overall architecture description are clear enough to follow.
weaknesses: The central originality claim of being 'the first any-to-any multimodal language model built entirely on mask-based discrete diffusion' is questionable: the paper itself cites highly related concurrent work such as Lumina-DiMOO ('omni diffusion large language model for multi-modal generation and understanding', [43]), MMADA [45], and DIMPLE [51], yet none of these are compared numerically, and the novelty relative to them is not delineated.

No ablation studies are provided for any of the proposed techniques (attenuated tail-pad masking, three-stage pipeline, position penalty, special token pre-infilling, adaptive token length), even though these are explicitly listed as key contributions. It is therefore impossible to attribute the reported gains to the proposed components.

The comparison set is thin and outdated: the primary any-to-any baselines are AnyGPT and NExT-GPT. Stronger, more relevant recent unified/omni models (e.g., Qwen2.5/3-Omni, VITA/VITA-1.5, Show-o, MMADA, Lumina-DiMOO, DIMPLE) are missing, making the 'comparable or better than existing multimodal systems' claim weakly supported.

Some claims are overstated or misleading. The abstract/Table 1 caption describe ASR performance as 'comparable' to specialized speech models, but 7.05 WER vs. GLM-4-Voice's 2.82 is ~2.5x worse. Similarly, text-to-image CLIP-T of 0.235 is below Emu's 0.286, yet the text emphasizes 'superior text-image alignment' based only on a comparison to NExT-GPT (0.225).

Speech evaluation is limited to WER computed via Whisper (intelligibility only); no naturalness/speaker-similarity metrics (e.g., MOS, SECS) are reported, and spoken visual understanding is only shown qualitatively in Fig. 4 with no quantitative benchmark.

Speech-to-image generation is evaluated only for efficiency (Tab. 3) and in the same-condition text/speech comparison (Tab. 3/section 4.1), without a quantitative table against baselines; the qualitative examples (Fig. 5) cannot substitute for this.

Reproducibility is limited: the training mixture includes a large in-house dataset (2,000K) and relies on multiple external models (Dream-7B, MAGVIT-v2, SenseVoiceSmall, GLM-4-Voice), and no training compute, hardware, or wall-clock budget is reported.

Some implementation details are unclear or appear inconsistent: the position penalty uses N^T = L - 100, which would penalize most of a short (e.g., 256-token) sequence and seems inconsistent with the stated goal of only discouraging simultaneous front/back decoding; no justification or ablation is given.

Presentation issues: typographical/grammatical errors ('ridgidly', 'mod els' line-break, 'decrease' used where 'decreasing' is meant in Tab. 3), and several figures are low-resolution, making the qualitative evidence hard to assess.

strengths: The paper tackles an ambitious and timely problem: unifying text, image, and speech understanding/generation in a single mask-based discrete diffusion backbone rather than an autoregressive LLM.

The proposed three-stage training pipeline, SDVI dataset, and inference heuristics (position penalty, special-token pre-infilling, adaptive token length) are practical engineering contributions that could inspire future multimodal MDM work.

Some individual results are promising: VQA performance on POPE/MME/Seed-2-Plus is competitive with the older visual LLM baselines reported, TTS WER is close to CosyVoice, and qualitative examples demonstrate inpainting and few-step generation potential.
The paper provides high-level implementation details (backbone, tokenizers, datasets, optimizer hyperparameters) that make the system concept understandable and potentially extensible.
The idea of controlling generation order and format through mask initialization in a discrete diffusion model is interesting and worth further study.
weaknesses: The central novelty claim—'first any-to-any multimodal language model built entirely on mask-based discrete diffusion'—is overclaimed and unsupported. Closely related diffusion-based multimodal models (e.g., MMaDA, Dimple, LLaDA-V, Lumina-DiMoO, NExT-Omni) are cited but not empirically compared, and the system still depends on external non-diffusion tokenizers/decoders (MAGVIT-v2, SenseVoiceSmall, GLM-4-Voice).

None of the paper's key technical contributions are ablated. There is no evidence that the three-stage pipeline, attenuated tail-pad masking, position penalty, special-token pre-infilling, or adaptive token-length assignment improve over simpler alternatives.

The evaluation is weak and outdated. Baselines are older models (mPLUG-Owl, LLaVA, InstructBLIP, AnyGPT, NExT-GPT) rather than modern multimodal or diffusion-based systems; text-to-image evaluation uses only CLIP-T/CLIP-I and omits FID, human evaluation, or modern benchmarks such as GenEval/DPG-Bench; inpainting is qualitative only.

Speech results undermine the paper's claims. ASR WER is 7.05 versus 2.82 for GLM-4-Voice and far worse than modern ASR, yet the text describes the speech performance as comparable or improved. TTS is evaluated only by Whisper WER, without naturalness, speaker similarity, or human evaluation.

Text-to-image results are not clearly strong: CLIP-T 0.235 is below DreamLLM (0.238) and Emu (0.286), and CLIP-I 0.667 is below DreamLLM (0.697) and NExT-GPT (0.691), so the claim of comparability to specialized visual LLMs is not well supported.

Reproducibility is poor. There is no code/model release, no compute budget (GPU hours, batch size, training cost), no release or detailed description of the SDVI and in-house datasets, and no complete evaluation protocol/prompts.

The method is under-specified: it is unclear how modalities are interleaved, how special tokens are defined, how loss is balanced across modalities, how the model avoids modality imbalance, and how classifier-free guidance/repetition penalty are applied in detail.

The paper claims 'no modality-specific optimization' but uses modality-specific tokenizers, modality-specific three-stage training, and modality-specific inference heuristics, creating a contradiction with its unified-model narrative.

The probabilistic formulation asserts a joint distribution over multimodal tokens, but the training objective is a standard masked-token cross-entropy without an explicit any-to-any conditional factorization; there is no theoretical or empirical analysis showing that this yields the claimed unified alignment.
The 'sampling efficiency' claim is not substantiated: the paper reports CLIP/WER degradation as steps decrease but gives no wall-clock latency, throughput, or comparison to autoregressive baselines.
No limitations, broader-impact, or ethics discussion is provided. Constructing SDVI via voice cloning on GigaSpeech raises consent, privacy, and deepfake risks that are not addressed.

Presentation quality is uneven: typos such as 'mod-els', 'regidly', and 'LLaVA-OneVisual'; duplicate JourneyDB rows; a wrong citation for Common Voice 17; inconsistent table footnotes; and several textual claims that do not match the reported numbers.
The lack of error bars, statistical tests, and failure-case analysis makes it difficult to judge whether small differences are meaningful.
The SDVI dataset is small (30K+30K) and the spoken visual interaction capability is demonstrated mainly with qualitative examples rather than quantitative benchmarks.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel architectural direction: an any-to-any multimodal model (text, speech, image) built entirely on a mask-based discrete diffusion backbone, modeling the joint distribution over multimodal discrete tokens rather than bolting output heads onto an autoregressive LLM.

The training and inference techniques are thoughtfully designed and well-motivated: three-stage progressive alignment, attenuated tail-pad masking for variable-length generation, position penalty for image repetition, special-token pre-infilling for speech, and adaptive token-length initialization.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering ASR, TTS, VQA (POPE/MME/Seed-2-Plus), text-to-image, speech-to-image, spoken visual QA, and inpainting, giving a reasonably complete picture of the system's capabilities.

Clearly demonstrates the practical advantages of the diffusion backbone over autoregressive models: strong performance with as few as 10-50 sampling steps and zero-shot inpainting without task-specific fine-tuning.
Writing is generally clear, figures are informative, and the pipeline/dataset construction (SDVI) is described in sufficient detail to follow the recipe.
weaknesses: The paper omits comparisons to the most directly relevant concurrent work: other mask-based discrete diffusion multimodal models (MMaDA, DIMpLE, LLaDA-V, Lumina-DiMOO) and unified models such as Show-o. These are cited in related work but never benchmarked against, which substantially weakens the central claim about the promise of diffusion backbones for multimodal intelligence.

The headline claim that Omni-Diffusion 'outperforms or performs on par' is not fully supported by the reported numbers: text-to-image CLIP-T (0.235) is below Emu (0.286) and only on par with DreamLLM (0.238), and ASR WER (7.05) is considerably worse than the speech LLM GLM-4-Voice (2.82). The strongest claims rest on the weakest evidence.

Evaluation protocol consistency is questionable. Several baseline numbers are borrowed from other papers or marked as re-implemented ('*'), and it is unclear whether datasets, prompts, decoders, and metrics are matched across methods, making the comparisons hard to trust as apples-to-apples.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or model checkpoint release is stated, it is unclear whether the SDVI dataset will be public, the 2000K 'in-house dataset' used for VQA is entirely undescribed, and no training compute/scale information is provided.
The 'first any-to-any' framing is somewhat overstated given the rapid concurrent work in this space, and the paper would benefit from a precise statement of what is novel relative to those systems.

Minor presentation issues (e.g., 'regidly' for 'rigidly', inconsistent 'DIMpLE' capitalization, 'LLaVA-OneVisual' vs 'LLaVA-OneVision', and a likely indexing typo N_t in the image token sequence) suggest the manuscript needs a careful proofread.

strengths: Introduces Omni-Diffusion, an any-to-any multimodal language model built on a mask-based discrete diffusion backbone that jointly models text, speech, and image discrete tokens; this is a meaningful exploration of non-autoregressive multimodal architectures.

Unified discrete-token joint modeling avoids a separate autoregressive LLM or external output diffusion model for each modality, and supports bi-modal and tri-modal tasks such as ASR, TTS, VQA, text-to-image, speech-to-image, and spoken visual question answering.

Proposes several tailored training and inference techniques: a three-stage progressive training pipeline, an SDVI dataset for speech-driven visual interaction, attenuated tail-pad masking for variable-length generation, position penalty for image generation, special token pre-infilling for spoken dialogue, and adaptive token-length assignment for ASR/TTS.

Reports competitive results on several benchmarks, including TTS WER 3.07 on LibriTTS, VQA results such as POPE 76.6 / MME-P 1216.7 / Seed-2-Plus 34.5, DPG-Bench 68.20, and sampling-efficiency gains with as few as 10 inference steps.

Demonstrates qualitative capabilities such as inpainting without additional fine-tuning and spoken visual interaction, which are promising advantages of masked discrete diffusion for multimodal generation.
weaknesses: Several central claims are overstated or inconsistent with the reported numbers. Table 1 states superior TTS performance compared to specialized speech models, but CosyVoice achieves lower WER (2.89 vs. 3.07). ASR WER is 7.05 versus GLM-4-Voice's 2.82, which is not 'comparable', and the abstract's broad claim that the method 'outperforms or performs on par' is only partially supported.

The evaluation lacks comparisons to recent and directly relevant omni-modal/unified systems, including VITA-1.5, Qwen3-Omni, Show-o, MMaDA, Lumina-DiMOO, and other 2025-2026 multimodal diffusion or any-to-any models, despite claiming broad comparisons across multimodal systems.

Many reported gains are marginal and lack statistical significance or confidence intervals, e.g., POPE 76.6 vs. LLaVA 76.3, MME-P 1216.7 vs. InstructBLIP 1212.8, and position-penalty ablation improvements of only +0.002 CLIP-T and +0.001 CLIP-I.

TTS evaluation is limited to WER measured via Whisper transcription, without MOS, speaker similarity, naturalness, or diversity metrics. ASR/TTS results are also restricted to LibriSpeech/LibriTTS, limiting conclusions about speech quality.

Speech-to-image and spoken VQA evaluations use speech synthesized by CosyVoice2, the same model used to construct the SDVI training data. This creates a potential distribution bias and does not test robustness to real human speech or other TTS systems.

Key technical components are not quantitatively ablated or analyzed: the three-stage training pipeline, attenuated tail-pad masking, adaptive token-length assignment, and special token pre-infilling are mainly justified qualitatively, and the position-penalty ablation shows only negligible gains.

Methodological details are insufficient for reliable reproduction: it is unclear how task sequences are formatted, whether input-modality tokens are masked during training, how classifier-free guidance and repetition penalty are applied, how the position-penalty hyperparameter N^t = L - 100 is intended to operate, and no training compute or resource details are reported.
Reproducibility is limited: no code or model weights are released, the 2M in-house dataset is unavailable, and the constructed SDVI dataset is not released despite being a core contribution.

The limitations discussion is very brief and does not address speech quality, hallucination, bias, synthetic-data artifacts, inference cost, dependence on pretrained tokenizers/encoders, or failure modes.

There are ethical concerns around voice cloning for SDVI construction from GigaSpeech samples and the generation of synthetic speech/images, but the paper does not discuss consent, potential misuse, or safeguards; the impact statement dismisses societal consequences.

The 'first any-to-any multimodal language model built entirely on mask-based discrete diffusion' claim may be overstated given related MDM/DFM-based omni-modal work such as NExT-Omni, Lumina-DiMOO, and MMaDA; the precise novelty boundary is not established.

Presentation issues reduce clarity, including typos ('LLaVA-OneVisual', 'caculated'), reference mismatches (e.g., Common Voice 17 cited as [32]), unclear table legends, and an omitted project webpage URL.

strengths: Ambitious and timely direction: attempts the first any-to-any multimodal LM built on mask-based discrete diffusion, unifying text, image, and speech understanding/generation in one backbone.

Integrates strong existing components (Dream-7B, MAGVIT-v2, SenseVoiceSmall, GLM-4-Voice) and proposes several practical techniques (attenuated tail-pad masking, position penalty, special-token pre-infilling, adaptive token-length assignment).
Broad empirical suite covering ASR, TTS, VQA, text-to-image, speech-to-image, spoken VQA, inpainting, sampling efficiency, and qualitative examples.
Some results are competitive: VQA POPE 76.6, MME 1216.7, Seed-2-Plus 34.5; TTS WER 3.07 vs GLM-4-Voice 5.64; few-step sampling and inpainting without fine-tuning are interesting.
The idea of using masked discrete diffusion for joint multimodal modeling is potentially useful and could inspire alternative non-autoregressive multimodal backbones.
weaknesses: Inconsistent central claim: Section 3.1 says all modalities are tokenized into discrete representations and jointly modeled, but speech input is actually encoded with SenseVoiceSmall continuous features and projected via an MLP adapter; the manuscript never explains how these continuous features enter the masked discrete diffusion loss. This undermines the claimed unified discrete joint distribution.

Missing most relevant recent diffusion-based multimodal baselines (MMaDA, Dimple, LLaDA-V, Lumina-DiMoO, NeXT-Omni, Fudoki). Without these comparisons, the 'first' and 'comparable/better than existing multimodal systems' claims are not substantiated; most baselines are older autoregressive or visual-only models.

Overstated results: ASR WER 7.05 is far worse than GLM-4-Voice's 2.82 yet called 'comparable'; TTS WER 3.07 is worse than CosyVoice's 2.89 yet called 'superior'/'comparable'; text-to-image CLIP-T 0.235 is below DreamLLM/Emu, and CLIP-I 0.667 is below NExT-GPT/DreamLLM, so claims of superior alignment/quality are not supported by the tables.

The 'any-to-any' evaluation is incomplete: no image-to-speech, image-to-text generation/captioning, or full multimodal conversation benchmark; spoken VQA is only MME questions converted to speech and has no baseline comparison. The paper does not establish arbitrary any-to-any capability.

Ablations are weak or absent: position penalty improves CLIP-T from 0.233 to 0.235 and CLIP-I from 0.666 to 0.667, likely within noise; special-token pre-infilling is supported only qualitatively; attenuated tail-pad masking and adaptive token-length assignment have no controlled ablations.

Method details are insufficient for reproducibility: masking schedule, how the mask ratio r is derived from t, sequence formatting/wrapping, loss weighting across modalities, classifier-free guidance and repetition penalty settings, and how continuous speech features interact with mask prediction are all unclear.

Reproducibility is poor: no code/model release statement, no compute budget, no random seeds, and training uses large proprietary/in-house data (e.g., 2M in-house VQA, 10M LAION-2B, 5,000 hours Emilia) plus synthesized SDVI data that is not described as released.

Ethical concerns around voice cloning: SDVI is created by cloning 1,000 randomly sampled GigaSpeech speakers, but the paper provides no evidence of consent, no discussion of deepfake/misuse risks, and only a generic impact statement. This is a material research-ethics gap.

Novelty is limited: the system largely integrates existing pretrained components (Dream-7B, MAGVIT-v2, SenseVoiceSmall, GLM-4-Voice) with heuristic training/inference tricks; entropy-based decoding is inherited from Dream-Instruct, and the conceptual contribution beyond prior discrete-diffusion multimodal work is incremental.

Presentation and table issues: duplicate JourneyDB rows in Table 4, typos such as 'LLaVA-OneVisual' and 'Laion-2B', incorrect citation for Common Voice 17 (cited as [32]), unexplained non-monotonic latency numbers (e.g., speech-to-image 256 steps 39.90 s vs 50 steps 7.74 s), and unclear/overstated claims in captions.

Inpainting and sampling-efficiency claims are not fairly supported: inpainting has no quantitative metric or baseline; few-step sampling reduces quality (CLIP-T 0.226 vs 0.235; CLIP-I 0.650 vs 0.667) and is compared to AR baselines with different quality/latency trade-offs, without FID or human evaluation.

Limitations discussion is inadequate: it only mentions future extension to visual editing, omitting the missing baselines, reproducibility constraints, speech-encoder inconsistency, ethical risks, and evaluation gaps.

The claim of 'no modality-specific optimization' is misleading: the model uses modality-specific tokenizers, encoders, adapters, and data mixtures, so modality-specific design is pervasive even if the loss is shared.

strengths: Introduces a novel any-to-any multimodal language model built entirely on mask-based discrete diffusion, modeling a joint distribution over text, image, and speech discrete tokens with a unified mask-token prediction objective. This is a meaningful architectural extension of MDMs beyond text/image domains.

Develops a three-stage progressive training pipeline and constructs the SDVI dataset for spoken visual QA and speech-to-image generation, enabling complex cross-modal tasks that require joint speech-vision-text reasoning.

Proposes several practical MDM-specific techniques: attenuated tail-pad masking for variable-length generation, position penalty for image generation, special token pre-infilling for spoken dialogue, and adaptive token length assignment for ASR/TTS.

Visual understanding results are competitive: POPE 76.6, MME-Perception 1216.7, and Seed-2-Plus 34.5, outperforming existing any-to-any models such as AnyGPT and NExT-GPT and approaching specialized visual LLMs like InstructBLIP.

Image generation on DPG-Bench reaches 68.20, competitive with SD v2.0 (68.09) and Show-o (67.48), demonstrating that the unified discrete diffusion model can produce reasonable images without an external diffusion decoder.

Demonstrates useful MDM advantages such as inpainting without additional fine-tuning and flexible speed-quality trade-offs via parallel decoding, e.g., 10 inference steps yields CLIP-T 0.226 vs 0.235 at 256 steps while reducing latency from 28.57s to 1.29s.
The paper is generally well organized, with clear architecture and training pipeline diagrams that make the proposed system understandable.
weaknesses: The central claim that Omni-Diffusion outperforms or performs on par with existing multimodal systems is overstated. ASR WER on LibriSpeech is 7.05 vs GLM-4-Voice 2.82, which is far worse, not comparable. TTS WER on LibriTTS is 3.07 vs CosyVoice 2.89, so it is not superior to the specialized TTS baseline. Text-to-image CLIP-T is 0.235 vs Emu 0.286 and DreamLLM 0.238, and CLIP-I is 0.667 vs NExT-GPT 0.691 and DreamLLM 0.697.

Important recent any-to-any and multimodal diffusion baselines are missing from the main comparisons, including VITA-1.5, Qwen2.5/3-Omni, Show-o, MMaDA, LLaDA-V, Dimple, and Lumina-DiMOO. Without these, the state-of-the-art positioning of the method is unclear.

Ablation evidence is weak. The position penalty improves CLIP-T only from 0.233 to 0.235 and CLIP-I from 0.666 to 0.667, which is marginal. Special token pre-infilling is supported only qualitatively. There are no quantitative ablations for attenuated tail-pad masking, the three-stage training pipeline, or adaptive token length assignment, so several design choices remain insufficiently justified.

Spoken VQA performance degrades substantially when speech is the input: Speech+Image-to-Text scores 1019.9 vs Text+Image-to-Text 1216.7, and Speech+Image-to-Speech scores 1004.6. This gap is not analyzed and weakens the claim of strong spoken visual interaction.

Limitations and ethics discussion is minimal, essentially one sentence. The paper does not discuss voice-cloning consent, potential misuse of synthesized voices, data contamination, or error propagation from ASR, despite constructing a dataset via voice cloning from GigaSpeech. The impact statement saying no consequences need highlighting is insufficient given these concerns.

Reproducibility is limited. The in-house 2000K VQA dataset is not described as released, training compute is not reported, and code/checkpoint availability is unclear from the paper. While hyperparameters and dataset lists are provided, full reproduction would be difficult.

The first any-to-any MDM claim may be challenged by concurrent work, and the paper should more carefully position itself against closely related systems such as MMaDA, Dimple, LLaDA-V, and Lumina-DiMOO, even if they differ in modality coverage or diffusion formulation.

Some presentation issues reduce clarity, including typos such as OneVisual instead of LLaVA-OneVision, Test Transcription instead of Text Transcription in figures, and NExt-OMNI in the references. Details such as the relation between mask ratio r and time step t, the exact position penalty schedule, and the choice of 0.25L for special token pre-infilling are not fully explained.
